edition.title: Morning Edition
edition.dek: A complicated carbon decline, Botswana's diamond ambitions, Germany's remembrance, and the question of intelligence without a brain.

lead_story.headline: Global fossil-fuel emissions edge down, but total carbon pollution still rises
lead_story.summary: Global Carbon Project researchers estimate fossil-fuel CO₂ emissions will fall 0.4% in 2026, mainly because the Iran war disrupted oil and gas supplies. Coal emissions rose, and emissions from land-use change pushed total global CO₂ emissions up roughly 1%. These are projections, not final annual measurements.
lead_story.why_it_matters: A crisis-driven decline is not the same as durable decarbonization; the distinction matters as COP31 begins.

items.headline: Botswana seeks a larger stake in the diamond business that shaped its economy
items.summary: President Duma Boko says Botswana intends to raise its De Beers ownership to 30% if a proposed consortium acquisition proceeds. The transaction remains proposed, and natural-diamond demand is under pressure from lab-grown alternatives.
items.why_it_matters: A resource-producing country is trying to capture more control and value from a major industry rather than merely supply raw materials.

items.headline: Germany marks Kristallnacht amid a rise in reported antisemitic incidents
items.summary: At a Munich synagogue, Chancellor Friedrich Merz warned that protecting Jewish life remains a test of Germany's democratic commitments. Monitoring group RIAS recorded 8,725 antisemitic incidents last year, though incident reporting is not identical to a complete count of offenses.
items.why_it_matters: The anniversary links the memory of state-sponsored persecution to the present obligation to protect minority communities.

items.headline: Science fiction wins the Booker Prize for the first time
items.summary: M. John Harrison, 81, won the 2026 Booker Prize for The End of Everything, a short postapocalyptic novel set on the Kent coast. The judges praised its literary ambition and unexpected humor.
items.why_it_matters: The award challenges the boundary between literary prestige and speculative fiction, where Harrison has worked for decades.

items.headline: A submerged Egyptian palace yields an image of an ancient lighthouse
items.summary: Archaeologists working near Alexandria recovered a bronze ring engraved with what researchers identify as the Lighthouse of Alexandria. Its image may help compare the ancient monument's representation in different media, although interpretations of small details remain tentative.
items.why_it_matters: A small personal object can illuminate how an enormous lost landmark was imagined and circulated in antiquity.

items.headline: Researchers assemble unusually precise molecular structures that support neurons in culture
items.summary: Northwestern researchers report giant self-assembled molecular structures with controlled lengths and charge patterns. In cell-culture experiments the materials promoted neuron organization and synapse formation; no human treatment has been demonstrated.
items.why_it_matters: Precisely structured materials may eventually help regenerative medicine, but laboratory cell behavior is an early step.

items.headline: An Alexandria library collects handmade winter items for neighbors
items.summary: Alexandria Library's Yarn Storm collection began November 9, inviting residents to donate handmade winter accessories through December 2 for Community Lodgings. It is a modest local service project organized around everyday skills.
items.why_it_matters: The ordinary work of knitting, giving and sharing a library space deserves a place alongside international headlines.

items.headline: Can a creature without a brain be intelligent?
items.summary: A reported essay follows scientists who study slime moulds that navigate, adapt and form efficient networks. It explores a disagreement between researchers who regard cognition as a broad biological capacity and those who reserve it for nervous systems.
items.why_it_matters: The disagreement exposes how definitions can shape experiments and what kinds of behavior scientists count as evidence of mind.

worth_your_time.headline: Why the promised revolution in cultivated meat has been slow
worth_your_time.summary: A long reported investigation revisits the early promise of cell-cultured meat and the practical barriers to scaling it: cost, manufacturing, consumer acceptance and regulatory hurdles.
worth_your_time.why_it_matters: It is a case study in how a technically possible innovation can remain economically and institutionally difficult.

daily_wonder.title: A storm wider than Earth
daily_wonder.caption: Voyager 2 photographed Jupiter's Great Red Spot on June 29, 1979, from more than nine million kilometers away. The storm sits amid bands of turbulent clouds, with smaller white ovals nearby; this is a NASA/JPL color composite.
daily_wonder.alt: Close view of Jupiter's tan and cream cloud bands with the oval Great Red Spot at right and smaller pale storms below.
daily_wonder.rights: Public domain in the United States (NASA work)

reflection.passage: What do we live for, if it is not to make life less difficult to each other?
reflection.author: George Eliot
reflection.context: Dorothea says this while defending the disgraced physician Lydgate against assumptions of guilt. Her question is not detached optimism; it challenges friends to offer practical loyalty before judging a person they know.
reflection.question: When has someone made a difficult part of your life easier, and what did that require of them?

https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.question: Does intelligence require a brain, or can adaptive behavior itself count as cognition?
https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.thesis: One side argues that flexible, history-sensitive problem-solving in organisms such as slime moulds warrants a broad biological concept of cognition; critics insist the term must be narrow enough to discriminate among mechanisms.
https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.argument: Slime moulds respond to gradients, alter networks and sometimes exploit traces of prior movement. Proponents treat these capacities as primitive cognition; skeptics argue chemical feedback can explain them without invoking mental states.
https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.intellectual_background: The debate contrasts nervous-system-centered theories with embodied, distributed and biogenic approaches to mind; defining intelligence by human-like reasoning would beg the question.
https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.example: A slime mould's route through a maze may improve after repeated exploration even though it has no neurons.
https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.strongest_objection: If every adaptive process is called intelligent, the term loses explanatory force; a thermostat could qualify.
https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.possible_response: Proponents can specify degrees of adaptive control, memory and environmental sensitivity, then test whether the framework predicts new behavior.
https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.implications: Definitions influence which organisms are studied and which experiments count as tests of learning.
unresolved_questions: What evidence distinguishes memory from a physical trace?
Can a useful scientific category be graded rather than binary?
